\chapter{Storm, Thunder And Ice}
\label{ch:la-tormenta-y-el-trueno}
\hlchaptermodality{370}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can say la tormenta, el trueno, el hielo, la cueva and la costa, and say what the weather is doing and where I am standing while it does it.}

Complete ES-C370-costa: say what the weather is doing and where you are standing while it does it.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[la tormenta]{la tormenta — weather that wrings the sky}

\label{lesson:ES-C370-tormenta}



\begin{quote}
Say \emph{smoke}, then \emph{ash}. (\emph{El humo}; \emph{la ceniza}.)
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item la nube — what one is made of.
  \item el viento — what arrives with it.
\end{itemize}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{tor-MEN-ta}, three beats with the weight on the second. The \emph{r} before the \emph{m} is a single tap, not a roll. $\to$ pronunciation reference
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{la tormenta} — \textquotedblleft{}the storm.\textquotedblright{}

Behind it is Latin \textbf{torquēre}, to twist or wring, and a noun \textbf{tormentum} built from it: a twisting.

A \emph{tormentum} was first a machine. Roman artillery stored its power in ropes of twisted sinew, wound tighter and tighter until they were let go. The twisting was the engine.

From there the word travels by short steps, and English took a piece at each stop:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{torment} and \textbf{torture} — what a twisting machine does to a person;
  \item \textbf{contort} and \textbf{distort} — twisted out of shape;
  \item \textbf{tortuous} — a road that twists;
  \item \textbf{torque} — the engineer's word for twisting force, taken off the Latin in the nineteenth century when machines needed a name for it again.
\end{itemize}

And \emph{tormenta}, the weather. A storm is the sky being wrung.

One caution, because it catches people. Spanish \textbf{torno} and \textbf{turno} look as though they belong to this family and do not. They come from a Greek word for a \textbf{lathe}, a completely separate line. Turning and twisting are near enough in sense to make the mistake feel safe, which is exactly why it is not.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
You can now say what the weather is doing: \emph{hay tormenta}.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{la tormenta}
  \item \emph{hay tormenta}
  \item \emph{una tormenta con viento}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What did a Roman \emph{tormentum} twist? (Ropes of sinew, in a catapult.) And do \emph{torno} and \emph{turno} belong to this family? (No — they come from a Greek word for a lathe.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[el trueno]{el trueno — the noise that reshaped an English word}

\label{lesson:ES-C370-trueno}



\begin{quote}
Say \emph{ash}, then \emph{the storm}. (\emph{La ceniza}; \emph{la tormenta}.)
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item la tormenta — what brings it.
  \item la luz — the flash that comes first.
\end{itemize}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{TRUE-no}, two beats with the weight on the first. The \emph{ue} is one glide, not two beats, and the \emph{tr} runs together. $\to$ pronunciation reference
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{el trueno} — \textquotedblleft{}thunder.\textquotedblright{}

The verb is \textbf{tronar}, to thunder, and it comes straight from Latin \textbf{tonāre}. The noun \emph{trueno} comes from a Latin noun for a thunderclap — with an extra \emph{r} that wandered in from a neighbouring Latin word for thunder and never left. Words borrow letters from their neighbours the way people borrow habits.

English holds \emph{tonāre} in three places, and only the first is obvious:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{detonate} — to thunder down;
  \item \textbf{astonish} — from a late Latin compound meaning to thunder \textbf{at} somebody. To astonish was to leave a person the way a thunderclap leaves them;
  \item \textbf{stun} — the same word again, worn shorter on its way through French. To stun and to astonish are one word at two lengths.
\end{itemize}

English \textbf{thunder} is not borrowed at all. It came down the Germanic line from the same ancient root, which is also where the god \textbf{Thor} gets his name — the thunderer.

The best of the family is one English took \textbf{from Spanish and got wrong}. A \emph{tronada} is a thunderstorm. English sailors brought the word home, and somewhere along the way its letters were shuffled into \textbf{tornado} — most likely under the pull of \emph{tornar}, \textquotedblleft{}to turn,\textquotedblright{} a different Spanish word that happened to describe exactly what the wind was doing. A mishearing that improved the word.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
You can now name both halves of a storm: \emph{el trueno y la luz}.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{el trueno}
  \item \emph{un trueno}
  \item \emph{hay truenos en la tormenta}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which English word is \emph{astonish} the shorter twin of? (\emph{Stun}.) And what Spanish word is \emph{tornado} a mangling of? (\emph{Tronada}, a thunderstorm.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[el hielo]{el hielo — an h that stands for nothing}

\label{lesson:ES-C370-hielo}



\begin{quote}
Say \emph{the storm}, then \emph{thunder}. (\emph{La tormenta}; \emph{el trueno}.)
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item la nieve — its softer neighbour.
  \item el frío — the condition that makes it.
\end{itemize}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{HIE-lo}, two beats with the weight on the first. The \emph{h} is silent and the \emph{ie} is one glide, so the word starts on a \emph{y}-like sound. $\to$ pronunciation reference
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{el hielo} — \textquotedblleft{}ice.\textquotedblright{}

Latin \textbf{gelū}, frost. English has the family wherever something sets as it cools:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{gelid}, taken straight off the Latin, meaning icy;
  \item \textbf{congeal}, to freeze together, through French;
  \item \textbf{jelly}, through French \emph{gelée}, a thing that has set;
  \item \textbf{gelatin}, through Italian and then French — the same word again, arriving a third time by a third road.
\end{itemize}

Now the letter at the front, because it is a different animal from the \emph{h} on \emph{humo}.

\emph{Humo} has an \emph{h} standing in for a Latin \textbf{f}. \emph{Hielo} does not: \emph{gelū} has no \emph{f} in it anywhere. That \emph{h} is a \textbf{spelling habit}. Medieval scribes wrote \emph{u} and \emph{v} with the same letter, so a word beginning \emph{ue-} was liable to be read as though it began with a consonant. Sticking an \emph{h} on the front settled the question, and the habit spread to \emph{ie-} as well.

That is why \textbf{huevo} and \textbf{hueso} carry one too. Latin \emph{ōvum} and \emph{ossum} have no \emph{f} to stand for either.

So Spanish has two silent \emph{h}'s doing two unrelated jobs. Do not generalise from one to the other: \textbf{hierro}, iron, comes from \emph{ferrum}, and its \emph{h} is the \emph{humo} kind after all.

One relative that will not come quietly: \textbf{glaciar}. It looks like it belongs with \emph{hielo}, and specialists cannot show that it does — the Latin word behind it resists being derived from \emph{gelū}. Near in meaning, unproven in ancestry.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
You can now name what cold water becomes: \emph{el hielo}.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{el hielo}
  \item \emph{con hielo}
  \item \emph{un café con hielo}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Does the \emph{h} of \emph{hielo} stand in for a Latin \emph{f}? (No — it is a spelling habit, like the one on \emph{huevo}.) And what does \emph{jelly} have in common with \emph{hielo}? (Both come from \emph{gelū}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[la cueva]{la cueva — the hollow, and one word that only looks hollow}

\label{lesson:ES-C370-cueva}



\begin{quote}
Say \emph{thunder}, then \emph{ice}. (\emph{El trueno}; \emph{el hielo}.)
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item la montaña — what one is usually inside.
  \item la sombra — what there is a lot of in there.
\end{itemize}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{CUE-va}, two beats with the weight on the first. The \emph{cu-} is a hard \emph{k} with a \emph{w} glide, and the \emph{v} is the same soft sound as a Spanish \emph{b}. $\to$ pronunciation reference
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{la cueva} — \textquotedblleft{}the cave.\textquotedblright{}

Latin \textbf{cavus} meant hollow. Spoken Latin also had a variant \textbf{cova}, and that is what Spanish grew \emph{cueva} out of — the stressed vowel breaking into \emph{ue}, which is why the word has a glide the Latin never did.

The family is wide, and every member is still hollow:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{cave} itself, which reached English through French;
  \item \textbf{cavity} and \textbf{excavate}, taken off the Latin;
  \item \textbf{cage}, from \emph{cavea}, a hollow enclosure for keeping animals;
  \item \textbf{gabion}, the wicker basket packed with earth that soldiers stack for cover — the same \emph{cavea}, come through Italian, still a hollow container.
\end{itemize}

And then the one to refuse. English \textbf{cove} — a small sheltered bay — looks like it must be \emph{cova} with the vowel worn down. It is not. \emph{Cove} is Old English \emph{cofa}, a small chamber, a Germanic word with no Latin in it; the seaside meaning is a late arrival, not turning up until the sixteenth century.

Two words for a hollow place, from two families, meeting in the middle by accident. Spanish caves and English coves are neighbours who are not related.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
You can now say where the shelter is: \emph{la cueva está en la montaña}.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{la cueva}
  \item \emph{una cueva}
  \item \emph{la cueva está en la montaña}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What did Latin \emph{cavus} mean? (Hollow.) And is English \emph{cove} from the same word? (No — it is Germanic, \emph{cofa}, a small chamber.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[la costa]{la costa — the country's rib}

\label{lesson:ES-C370-costa}



\begin{quote}
Say \emph{ice}, then \emph{the cave}. (\emph{El hielo}; \emph{la cueva}.)
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item el mar — what it holds back.
  \item la isla — a place that is all of it.
\end{itemize}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{COS-ta}, two beats with the weight on the first. The \emph{st} is a clean \emph{s} against a \emph{t} on the teeth, with no vowel in front of the \emph{s}. $\to$ pronunciation reference
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{la costa} — \textquotedblleft{}the coast.\textquotedblright{}

Latin \textbf{costa} is a \textbf{rib}. Not the sea, not the shore — a bone in your side.

The step to a coastline is a picture rather than a definition. A rib is the \textbf{side} of a body; a coast is the side of a country. English took the same picture and uses it every day without opening it up:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{coast}, from the Latin through French;
  \item \textbf{intercostal}, the muscles between the ribs, straight off the Latin;
  \item to \textbf{accost} — \emph{ad} plus \emph{costa}, to come up alongside. You accost somebody by arriving at their side;
  \item \textbf{cutlet}, which is French \emph{côtelette}, a diminutive of a diminutive: a little little rib. English speakers pulled its first syllable towards \textbf{cut} because a cutlet is something cut, and the word has looked like that ever since.
\end{itemize}

There is a footnote about the Spanish word itself. \emph{Costa} did not come down the inherited line into Castilian; it was taken in from a neighbouring language of the peninsula. The form that \textbf{did} come down the inherited line is \textbf{cuesta}, a slope — with the broken vowel that marks an inherited word. One Latin rib, two Spanish words, and the diphthong tells you which is which.

Two neighbours that are nothing to do with it: \textbf{cosa}, a thing, and \textbf{cosecha}, a harvest. Both begin the same and neither is a relative.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
You can now say where the land stops: \emph{la costa del mar}.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{la costa}
  \item \emph{la costa del mar}
  \item \emph{la casa está en la costa}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does Latin \emph{costa} mean? (A rib.) And which Spanish word is the inherited form of it? (\emph{Cuesta}, a slope.)
\end{tcolorbox}
